facebook.content_angle: Pull buoy dependency — how leaning on pull buoys masks a broken body position and weak kick timing, leaving swimmers slower when the buoy comes off
facebook.post_text:
Your pull buoy is lying to you. 🎯

Most swimmers feel faster with a pull buoy — and they are. But that speed is borrowed. The moment it comes off, the drag returns, the hips drop, and the times reflect it.

Here's what's actually happening:
👉 The buoy artificially lifts your hips, masking a body position you haven't earned
👉 Your legs stop contributing — and your kick timing slowly deteriorates
👉 Race day arrives and your stroke falls apart in the back half

The pull buoy isn't the problem. Over-relying on it is. 💥

Elite swimmers use it as a specific tool — not a comfort blanket. If you can't hold your stroke shape without it, that's the training gap to close first.

✔️ Limit pull sets to 20% of total yardage
✔️ Film your body position with and without the buoy — the difference will surprise you
✔️ Add kick-focused sets specifically to rebuild the leg timing the buoy has been hiding

How much of your current training relies on the pull buoy?
